Our faculty and staff are collegial and have demonstrated willingness to plan and adapt in light of new
challenges and opportunities. The department has been actively working to improve our student reach
and our campus, regional, and national reputation.

Major Findings

The self-study has provided valuable opportunity for reflection and planning as our department
embraces a new applied/career-based focus. The study underscores our perceived need to update and
optimize program offerings to attract students in an era of declining resources. Recent rertirements
leave us unable to continue strong undergraduate and MA-level offerings in archaeology related to
North America and Cultural Resources Management. The viability of the CRM Certificate is a new
concern, and we are missing opportunities to meet student demand for MA training in CRM
acchaeology, an historic strength of our department. We’ve learned, however, that student interest, plus
ECU’s investment in a new forensic anthropologist, has allowed significant growth in biological/forensic
anthropology: SCH generation in our Intro. to Biological Anthropology (ANTH/BIOL 2015) course
increased from 495 in 18/19 to 771 in 23/24 and 1533 in 24/25, and strong bio/forensic anthropology
interest has allowed our MA program to grow despite our recent inability to train CRM archaeologists.

The self-study has also allowed ample consideration of departmental needs in terms of personnel,
resources, curricular change and more significant community engagement as a high-impact learning
practice. Finally, the study highlights the strong teaching, research and service work already being
done by our faculty, providing exemplars for good work ahead.

1.1. Program Purpose (BA)
The East Carolina University (ECU) Department of Anthropology offers a global view of human culture,
evolution, adaptation, and history to promote comparative understanding of the archaeological,
biological, and cultural aspects of humanity. To  g  e  t  h  e  r  ,  these studies nurture respect for the biological as
well as the ethnic and cultural variation present in human populations today and throughout time.

BA Anthropology students are prepared to serve society by applying methods of anthropological inquiry
across a wide and ever-emerging array of problems, questions, and career paths. Our degree program
enables students to recognize the diversity of the world’s peoples (past and present), prepares them to
be effective at communicating cross-culturally and within multicultural settings, and equips them to
apply the critical thinking skills and knowledge learned in Anthropology to a broad array of careers in
local and global settings. Students have access to high impact learning practices specific to
anthropological subdisciplines, allowing them to further develop desirable career and citizenship skills.

1.2. Program Alignment (BA)
Student Success: Anthropologists are problem solvers, and our department aspires to train students
to manage complex challenges in workplaces and communities today, but also to identify, assess and
solve problems through the decades as their careers and lives unfold. Our focus on career
development, outreach, and skills training is designed to give students the methodological tools to
succeed in a broad array of domains of application, whether those students are seeking broad
anthropological training (such as in our BA or MA) or more narrow focus aligned with another program
of study (such as our Anthropology minor, Medical Anthropology minor, or certificates in Cultural
Resources Management, Forensic Anthropology, or Global Cross-Cultural Competency). We are
actively refining our curricula to achieve alignment with our vision and have begun the process with a
faculty retreat and participation in the Anthropology Career Readiness Network’s Departmental
Advisory Initiative (ACRN DAI).

Our time to degree is low and surveyed students report high levels of postgraduate success
(employment or post-graduate education), though response rates are lower than we’d like. About a
quarter of our students are first generation college students and well over half of them have unmet
financial needs. The skills and credentials we provide to our students are substantial contributors to
social and economic mobility.

Public Service: Anthropology by its very nature promotes the values of cultural understanding in the
campus community and the region. Our general education courses expand the world for hundreds of
ECU students each year. Our faculty and students conduct research that helps the public through
facilitating sustainable coastal development, reducing regional health disparities, historically
contextualizing human disease, helping solve medicolegal death investigations, advancing
understanding of human biological and behavioral diversity through research on primates and human
populations, and fostering appreciation of regional and international cultural heritage. Our graduates
are working in a broad array of positions in cultural resource management, education, social services,
health, and technology in private and state and federal government sectors, each of which contributes
to a strong departmental legacy of applying the anthropological endeavor in service to local and global
publics.

Regional Transformation: Growth in our region requires anthropologists. Cultural Resource
Management (CRM) archaeologists conduct required surveys before new highways, schools, and other
publicly-funded facilities are built. Cultural anthropologists with expertise in community development
manage social services agencies and help businesses attract and retain clients. Biological
anthropologists help with death investigation, train law enforcement personnel, and provide sharp
research analyst skills in the bioengineering, medical and pharmaceutical sectors, among many others.
Medical anthropologists provide effective public health research and interventions that help us
understand and improve local health, thus reducing health expenditures for the region. Many of our
medical anthropologists go on to clinical health careers and positions of influence, as well, giving them
added capacity to care for increasingly complex patient needs and outcomes in a manner mindful of the
effects of culture on human health.

Anthropology is unique in its focus on preparing students to transform communities through careful
observation and planning that includes multiple viewpoints. While many of our graduates leave the
region, those who remain engage in careers that advance quality of life and economic growth in eastern
North Carolina. Further, our department takes pride in offering high impact and local and public-facing
educational opportunities through archaeological field schools; class projects with community agencies;
student engagement in medicolegal death and missing persons investigations; and local internships
with cultural resource management agencies, museums, and Medical Examiners. Our department’s
active faculty and student research fosters growth in eastern North Carolina, including improving rural
health and well-being; analyzing indicators of growth; discovering, developing, and interpretating
historic sites; working with community members to achieve balance in sustainability and viability of
coastal communities; and building community relationships to preserve local history.

1.3 Unique Features (BA)
Our program provides transformative experiences for students through high impact learning practices
that range from participating in forensic investigations to taking part in field experiences both locally and
abroad. We have engaged undergraduate students in research collaborations with faculty curating
archaeological collections, researching primate and human interactions, and engaging in health
services research. We have established a clear undergraduate internship pathway with the Queen
Anne’s Revenge Conservation Lab (run by the North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural
Resources, or NC DNCR) on ECU’s West Research Campus. We have ongoing study abroad
programs emphasizing field research in Medical Anthropology in Peru and Ethnoprimatology in Bali,
and until just this year we held an eastern North Carolina archaeological field school (for undergraduate
and graduate students) each summer. Anthropology has long been a major contributor to the Global
Understanding program at ECU, which enables our students to interact via videoconferencing and chat
with students from different cultures.

Our department largely focuses on three of the four major subfields in anthropology (cultural
anthropology, archaeology, and biological anthropology), although cross-listed coursework in linguistic
anthropology may be offered through the English Department based on faculty availability. Significant
planning and external collaboration efforts 24/25 helped us clarify a focus on applied anthropology as
articulated through enhanced discussion of careers and problem solving. We worked with the
Anthropology Career Readiness Network’s Departmental Advisory Initiative (ACRN DAI) to begin
planning and implementing curriculum and pedagogical transitions to this end. (Appendix A: ACRN DAI
Implementation Plan) The department benefits from anthropology’s interdisciplinary nature, which
creates bridges to other programs and academic pursuits. Two of our faculty have joint appointments:
one with Public Health and one with the Institute for Coastal Science Policy (ICSP). Faculty scholarship
additionally transforms the region through initiatives such as sustainable coastal development, reducing
health disparities, cultural heritage promotion, compliance with federal historical preservation laws, and
understanding of variation in human growth and development in eastern North Carolina. Our students

exacerbated by the retirement of two faculty members (in 2021), both cultural anthropologists who were
particularly strong in undergraduate student advising and recruitment, and whose lines were not

decrease, as well, since anthropology is a “discovery” major (a discipline that few students are exposed

Fall 24), such that statewide total BA enrollees across the three combined majors declined just 12.9%
over the study period (insight.northcarolina.edu). This growth in anthropology’s ability to effectively
serve students with interests in a career as a health professional is something the department is poised
to build upon.

1.5 Workforce Demand (BA)
The Bureau of Labor Statistics forecasts 8% (faster than average) growth in anthropologists and
archaeologists nationwide from 2023-33 (Bureau of Labor Statistics). While this outlook is positive, it
tells only part of our story. These predictions are jobs specifically hiring “anthropologists”, i.e.,
professional anthropologists, primarily in academia and the federal government. Although data are hard
to come by, most jobs well-suited for anthropology majors lack “anthropology” in the title.  This includes
employment  in non-governmental organizations; in community-based settings for non-profit agencies;
for local, state and federal government agencies; in the health sector; in the corporate and business
world (including in Cultural Resource Management); in historical interpretation and museums; in the
forensic sciences and associated disciplines; and in academia (research, teaching, administration)
(American Anthropological Association). Our career emphasis and ACRN DAI participation is yielding
tools to promote student career preparation across multiple domains of application, thus helping
students more effectively connect the skills we teach in our classrooms and labs to specific career
pathways.

1.8 Contribution to Critical Professions (BA)
ECU’s undergraduate anthropology program lays a foundation supporting the health, educational
attainment, and quality of life of North Carolinians. The Anthropology program utilizes an integrated
approach to cultural, biological, and archaeological anthropology courses, taught by caring faculty
with a focus on career preparation and high-impact educational practices. The undergraduate
Anthropology program contributes to the social science education and pre-professional degrees of
the future health professionals, mental health practitioners, public health experts, legal experts, and
educators who serve the people of North Carolina. The program holistically prepares helping
professionals by training them to creatively solve human problems whose solutions derive from an
integrated and holistic understanding of human culture, human biology, and the human past.
Whether entering the North Carolina job market right after graduation or continuing to a
professional/graduate program, students who have majored, minored, or even just taken a class or
two in Anthropology will contribute positively to the wellbeing of their fellow North Carolinians with
the problem-solving perspective they gain in our department.

MA Anthropology
1.1 Program Purpose (MA)
The Master of Arts in Anthropology is a competitive, research and skill-intensive graduate program that
provides graduates with in-depth training in three core areas of the discipline: cultural anthropology,
biological anthropology, and archaeology. Students also gain specialized skills tailored to their unique
interests, whether in statistics, public health, forensic anthropology, primatology, bioarchaeology,
archaeology and conservation, or allied topics.

Degree recipients are equipped with the experience and ability to immediately contribute to career
domains in CRM archaeology and heritage management, public health and social services, forensic
science, federal and state government analysis, and educational administration. Flexible tracks,
including internship and practicum options, aid in career preparation and complement traditional
research-based experience.

heavy metal toxins of nonhuman primates has highlighted how humans live among lemurs,

social services agencies, tech firms, medical research and death investigation, and in the corporate
world, or go on to pursue PhDs at other universities. ECU anthropology alumni are particularly well-
placed across the region and state in cultural resource management, conservation, historic
interpretation, and higher education administration.

In Spring 2024 the Anthropology MA program was flagged by the state for falling below a newly
constructed Return on Investment (RoI) threshold. Specifically, the MA Anthropology Program was
flagged via calculation of Student ROI. Calculations were limited to data from the four MA graduates in
19/20 residing in NC. The timing and limitations of the study thus excluded the successes of students
graduating before or after that year, or who found gainful and rewarding employment across the country
or the globe.  The designation afforded us the opportunity to create an improvement plan for time to
degree while showcasing our departmental commitment to strong student mentorship. We have revised
admissions review procedures and advising practices, enhanced alumni interaction/networking, and
enhanced graduate student support. Enhanced support includes an increase in assistantship amounts
from $10,000 to $14,000/academic year, conference registration funding for all presenting MA students,
and significant external fundraising to support the same. Additionally, in Fall 24 we instituted a “Midterm
Mentoring” program wherein all MA students meet with their advisor and the Graduate Director or Chair
each term to discuss current progress and any challenges, strategize thesis or non-thesis pathways
aligned with developing career aspirations, and receive advice for post-graduate preparation. These
improvements are all designed to ensure timely degree completion, but also to provide students with
clear mentorship, networking opportunities, and skills necessary to succeed on the job market.

1.8 Contribution to Critical Professions (MA)
The Anthropology MA program plays a vital role in advancing professions that improve health,
education, and quality of life across North Carolina. With advanced training in cultural, biological, and
archaeological anthropology, the program prepares graduates to work in, for example, public health,
forensic science, education, and community development.
More specifically, cultural anthropology students regularly research barriers to healthcare access in
rural communities and collaborate with local health departments on outreach related to chronic
illnesses like diabetes and heart disease. Archaeology students conduct research at significant state
sites, such as Tryon Palace and the Queen Anne’s Revenge shipwreck, often in response to public
agency requests. In addition, they facilitate regional development through cultural resources
management, facilitating compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act for
federal projects. Local cultural resource management firms such as SWCA Environmental Consultants
and Chronicle Heritage frequently employ our archaeology graduates, such that ECU is known by these
firms as a consistent source of prospective employees. Biological anthropology students assist law
enforcement and Medical Examiners with forensic investigations, applying their training in skeletal
analysis and patterns of decomposition to support public safety and justice. They also play a critical role
in analyzing archaeological skeletons for cultural resource management firms, including identifying
possible Native American ancestors that necessitate in further tribal or state-level coordination.
Moreover, many graduates remain in North Carolina to work in public serving positions, working as
educators, engaged in law enforcement, running museum programs, or contributing to historical
preservation.
Collectively, these efforts enhance awareness of and pride in our North Carolinian heritage, as well as
support regional tourism, education, health, and safety. Whether entering the workforce or pursuing
further study, graduates are well-equipped to serve and uplift North Carolina communities.

Certificate in Cultural Resources Management (CRM)
1.1. Certificate Purpose (CRM)
The premise of the CRM certificate is that changes in federal and state laws as well as public interest
over the last few decades have been significant enough to warrant development of an explicit program
aligning with archaeology becoming a professional applied career option.  Broadly speaking, when
completed, the certificate provides students with a basic level of competency to pursue an entry-level
job in either the public or private sector of archaeology or be equally prepared to continue their
education in graduate school. It includes skills preparation options in GIS and public history and
museum studies.

1.2 Certificate alignment (CRM)
When originally proposed, the certificate was created to correspond with at least one goal in ECU’s
strategic plan: “education for a new century.” To  d  a  y  ,  t  h  e  c  e  r  t  i  f  i  c  a  t  e  i  s  a  l  s  o  c  o  n  s  i  s  t  e  n  t  w  i  t  h  t  h  e  E  C  U  ’  s
goals of “maximizing student success” and “public service.” This certificate maximizes student success
by providing job training while also serving the public in that most of these jobs are related to historic
preservation—the latter being of keen interest to the public in the 21st century. In addition, CRM is
required by historic preservation laws and involves archaeologists employed by either federal or state
agencies or by private firms who assist in compliance with these laws.

1.3 Unique features (CRM)
This certificate is distinctive in that it is tailored to students in our archaeology program. As such, it can
be considered an “applied track.” It thus makes us more competitive with other universities by providing
students with a specific curriculum designed to provide them with the skills to pursue archaeology jobs
or a graduate degree.

The CRM certificate has had between 2 (Fall 18) and 10 (Fall 21) students enrolled during the study

and for our archaeological field school. The recent retirement of two NC archaeologists in the
department necessitated the cancellation of the field school for Summer 2025 and the foreseeable
future. Since the field school is a core component of the certificate we anticipate that CRM certificate
enrollment will quickly wane unless we are able to hire one or more archaeologists to focus on the local

Certificate in Forensic Anthropology
1.1  Certificate Purpose (Forensic)
The purpose of the Forensic Anthropology Certificate is to equip students with introductory skills and
knowledge leading toward competency in forensic anthropological application. These skills include
human anatomy, basic forensic science and evidence handling, expert witness testimony, professional
standardization and ethics, field recovery, determination of medicolegal significance, forensic
taphonomy, biological profile techniques leading towards personal identification, and the use of
statistics in human identification applications. Upon completion, the certificate provides students with a
basic level of competency applicable to entry-level jobs in either the public- or private sector in the field
of death investigation and/or broader forensic investigative practices. Further, completion of the
certificate prepares students for graduate training across anthropology or the forensic sciences and
provides the introductory skills necessary for professional training in medicine, dentistry, or nursing.

1.2 Certificate Alignment (Forensic)
The Forensic Anthropology Certificate directly contributes to the institution's mission by equipping
students with specialized skills that not only serve the local and global economy but also foster public
service and regional transformation. Through hands-on training and research, students help solve real-
world issues related to justice, public safety, and human rights, thereby improving quality of life locally
and globally. Further, and in line with regional transformation and the associated priority of outcomes in
rural communities, skills learned are translatable to a criminal justice / forensic science career paths in
local eastern NC medicolegal settings where specialized training may be lacking.

1.3 Unique Features (Forensic)
ECU was a pioneer in offering forensic anthropology certification to undergraduate students. Several
other universities now have similar programs, but our certificate continues to help us more clearly
attract students with interest in forensic anthropology, plus it allows students (particularly those with
interest in criminal justice or biology) to specialize in an anthropological sub-discipline. It also

Certificate in Global Cross-Cultural Competency
1.1 Certificate Purpose (Global CCC)
This certificate was developed and approved for the undergraduate curriculum in 2015. The required
course work is designed to provide students with the knowledge, skills, and attitudes that they will need
to work with people from different cultural backgrounds in both domestic and international settings.
When completed, the certificate provides students a basic level of competency to pursue an entry-level
job in a range of fields (e.g., business, education, health care, human and social services) or be equally
prepared to continue their education in graduate school. Through the certificate, students gain
knowledge and skills that will prepare them to understand differences across cultural groups and to
interact and collaborate effectively with diverse populations.

1.2 Certificate Alignment (Global CCC)
The Global Cross-Cultural Competency Certificate provides students with specialized knowledge and

differences is a critical skill that will allow for success in a broad array of career paths. For students to

contribute to workplaces that can benefit from multicultural understanding in problem-solving, service

BA-Anthropology
3.1 Degree Requirements (BA)
The BA in Anthropology prepares students with skills and perspectives needed to succeed in a
globalized world by fostering cross-cultural understanding and critical thinking. Students begin with
2000-level courses in cultural anthropology, archaeology, and biological anthropology (with a lab), then
advance to 3000- and 4000-level courses, including at least one required methods course and electives
on specialized topics. Students also complete a minor, foreign language study, and general education.
The program maintains high retention and graduation rates, strong student satisfaction, and consistent
four-year degree completion.

3.2 Approaches to Curriculum and Innovative Practices (BA)
The department keeps its curriculum current through regular faculty reviews, integration of new
research, and responsiveness to student feedback. Faculty assess course offerings, learning
outcomes, and program goals to ensure alignment with disciplinary developments and best practices.

The program emphasizes hands-on learning through field schools, laboratory experience, and
community project participation. Students gain experience in local initiatives such as the Ayden African
American Cemetery Project and the Bath historical archaeology field school, as well as international
programs in Medical Anthropology (Peru) and Ethnoprimatology (Bali). Laboratory training in
archaeology, biological anthropology, and forensics provides additional practical skills through work on
artifact curation, skeletal analysis, and primate research.

Global engagement is fostered through ECU’s Global Understanding program, which connects students
with peers worldwide for cross-cultural dialogue. The department also employs equitable teaching and
assessment practices, using inclusive materials, transparent assignments, and varied assessments
such as collaborative projects, reflective writing, and community-based research. These experiences
help students apply theory in real-world contexts and build professional competencies.

Student Learning Outcomes Assessment
3.3 Strengths and Weaknesses (BA)
Assessment shows strong student performance in cross-cultural understanding, theory application, and
hands-on research through fieldwork, labs, and global engagement, while also identifying areas for
improvement.

In Cultural Anthropology, 90% of students met the benchmark in 23/24, demonstrating solid
understanding of core concepts and methods. To strengthen kinship and the culture concept, additional
lectures and readings will be added to the senior capstone in 25/26, with assessment through quizzes
and exams.

In Biological Anthropology, only 48% met the benchmark in 23/24. While improvements were noted
in understanding evolutionary forces, gaps remain in hominin phylogeny and phylogenetics. Targeted
lectures and readings will address these in 25/26.

3.5 Changes Related to Assessment (BA)
The department regularly reviews student learning outcomes to guide curriculum, pedagogy, and
program development. Faculty analyze data, identify gaps, and implement targeted improvements,
maintaining rigor and transparency. Recent enhancements include:

Cultural Anthropology: Revised senior capstone with added lectures and readings on kinship, culture,
and marriage, using Anthropology (Hasty et al.), Window on Humanity (Kottak), and a tutorial (O’Neil).
Similar readings are acceptable.

Archaeology: Strengthened instruction on relative dating, Upper Paleolithic art, and the peopling of the
Americas through relatable examples and updated readings.

Biological Anthropology: Improved coverage of evolutionary forces, hominin phylogeny, and cognition,
drawing on O’Neil modules and Explorations: An Open Invitation.

Field schools, labs, and global programs remain integral, and assessment tools are being refined to
better capture knowledge and skills. These evidence-based decisions reflect the department’s ongoing
commitment to student success.

3.6 Effectiveness of Changes (BA)
The department has implemented changes based on assessment data, with measurable improvements
in some areas and ongoing challenges in others.

In Biological Anthropology, added lectures and readings improved student understanding of
evolutionary forces, though comprehension of hominin phylogeny remains below the benchmark,
suggesting further instructional refinements are needed. In Archaeology, students achieved perfect
scores on absolute dating and vertical excavation but continued to struggle with archaeological context
and index fossils. In Cultural Anthropology, students already exceeded benchmarks, and
enhancements on kinship, marriage, and the culture concept were added to deepen engagement, with
follow-up data forthcoming.

Assessment results reflect program-level trends rather than individual growth, as each year measures a
different student cohort. Longitudinal tracking remains an aspirational goal given current resources.

These efforts have strengthened foundational knowledge and demonstrate the department’s ongoing
dedication to continuous improvement.

Certificate in Cultural Resources Management
3.1 Degree Map and Course Sequences (CRM)
The Certificate in Cultural Resources Management (CRM) is designed to progressively build student
knowledge and skills through a structured sequence of prerequisites and advanced coursework.
Students must maintain a minimum 2.5 GPA for admission and throughout the program, which requires
at least 18 semester credit hours.

3.2 Approaches to Curriculum and Innovative Practices (CRM)
The CRM certificate curriculum has heretofore been kept current through faculty expertise, ongoing
engagement with the discipline, and integration of emerging technologies and legislation. Faculty
teaching the core courses — ANTH 3077 (Archaeological Methods) and ANTH 3175 (Archaeological
Field Training) — draw on extensive fieldwork and research experience to introduce students to
contemporary methods, tools, and legal frameworks.

Innovative approaches include using tools such as Google Earth to identify archaeological sites in arid
environments, incorporating the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990) and its
2023 revisions, and training students on field technologies like the total station.

diversity and global perspectives (ANTH 1050 and ANTH 2010), which serve as prerequisites for
ANTH 3050, where they develop and apply ethnographic methods. They then complete advanced
electives in specialized areas, ensuring a progression from broad understanding to methodological
competence and applied expertise.

3.2 Approaches to Curriculum and Innovative Practices (Global CCC)
The program maintains an up-to-date curriculum through annual review and the active engagement of
faculty in research and fieldwork, which ensures that emerging methodologies and disciplinary
developments inform instruction. Assessment results from the annual review are shared among faculty
and guide curricular improvements. The program also incorporates innovative and equitable teaching
practices, including field-based, culturally responsive, and community-engaged approaches that expose
students to diverse perspectives. Dr. Brooks integrates his field school in Peru to teach ethnographic
methods, while Dr. Grace-McCaskey uses her work with community groups such as ONE Carolina to
model ethical, community-centered research.

3.3 Learning Outcomes Assessment (Global CCC)
Assessment data show strong student achievement in understanding cultural beliefs, values, and
sensibilities. In 24/25, all students met the benchmark for distinguishing race as a cultural construct,
with an average score of 93%, demonstrating effective preparation for engaging a global society.

Weaknesses remain in related areas, including misunderstandings of sociologists’ roles, the sexual
division of labor in marriage, and the Hawaiian kinship system. In negotiation skills, only 67% met the
benchmark, with difficulties applying cultural relativism, identifying collaborative leadership strategies,
and recognizing religious freedom protections.

Overall, the curriculum supports foundational competencies needed for global engagement but would
benefit from stronger focus on negotiation, cultural relativism, and inclusive leadership.

3.6 Effectiveness of Changes (Global CCC)
The effectiveness of instructional changes varied by outcome. For Cultural Beliefs, Values, and
Sensibilities, emphasizing race as a cultural construct and distinguishing it from ethnicity was highly

Amendment and religious freedom fell short, with only 67% meeting the benchmark. Students struggled
to recognize protections for wearing a headscarf and to apply cultural relativism and collaborative
leadership. These results highlight progress in targeted areas while underscoring the need for
continued refinement to support student engagement with global and cultural complexities.

MA Program
3.1 Degree requirements (MA)
The MA program in Anthropology at ECU offers rigorous, applied training that prepares graduates for
both professional practice and further academic study. Students complete core coursework in
archaeology, biological, and cultural anthropology, along with applied skills courses and specialized
training aligned with their career goals.

Field-based learning is a cornerstone of the program. Summer field schools, internships, practicums,
and applied research provide students with hands-on experience and essential professional
competencies. A thesis option is also available for those pursuing research-focused careers.

The recent retirements of Professors Daniel and Ewen have reduced the department’s capacity in
Archaeology of North America, eliminating fieldwork in this area and decreasing applications from
students seeking such training. At the same time, growing expertise in biological and forensic
anthropology has expanded career pathways and attracted new students.

The program remains committed to continuous improvement, student success, and high standards of
graduate education.

3.2 Approaches to curriculum and innovative practices (MA)
The MA program in Anthropology maintains a rigorous, up-to-date curriculum through regular review
informed by faculty expertise, student feedback, and assessment data. Faculty integrate emerging
research, methods, and professional practices into coursework, drawing on their local, national, and
international fieldwork to keep instruction relevant and current. These experiences enrich classroom
learning and give students opportunities to engage directly in research and fieldwork alongside faculty.

Assessment results have driven meaningful improvements to curriculum and instruction. Previously,
students took all three core courses — archaeology, biological, and cultural anthropology — in their first
semester, which many found overwhelming. Students shared this with their advisers, the graduate
program director, and department chair (in a series of interviews he conducted in Spring 24). Faculty
also felt pressure under this arrangement, as poor student performance in core courses would likely
lead to removal from the program (as happened with one student in Fall 24, and had happened in prior
terms, as well). To improve student experience and retention, beginning in Fall 2025 we’re teaching just
two of the core courses each Fall (the third will be taught the following fall). We will stagger trailing
courses based largely on the interests of entering MA students. This change also offers course
flexibility in the fall term so that students can work toward methods skills (such as a four-term GIS
Certificate offered in the Department of Earth, Environment and Planning) or research experiences.

Faculty advisors work closely with each student to develop a personalized academic plan aligned with
their interests and career goals. The program offers flexible pathways to support diverse goals and
ensure equitable access, including practica, internships, non-thesis, and thesis options. These
practices promote student success and prepare graduates for both professional and academic
achievement.

Executive Summary

Program Quality

This Self-Study of the East Carolina University (ECU) Department of Anthropology begins with the
2018/2019 (18/19) academic year and encompasses two degree programs (BA Anthropology and MA
Anthropology) and three undergraduate certificate programs (Cultural Resources Management,
Forensic Anthropology, and Global Cross-Cultural Competency). We  o ff e r  u n d e r g r a d u a t e  m i n o r s  i n
Anthropology and in Medical Anthropology. The department has nine tenured and tenure-track faculty
members and two fixed-term faculty members, a reduction of three faculty members since the last self-
study conducted in 18/19. The department is building an applied, career-focused identity across our
programs. ECU’s Mission incorporates Student Success, Public Service, and Regional Transformation.
Our work across three fields (biological, cultural and archaeological anthropology) relates to the mission
as follows:

Student Success: In the BA, our time to degree is low (averaging 3.73 years between 17/18 and 23/24)
and surveyed students report high levels of postgraduate success (employment or post-graduate
education), though response rates are lower than we’d like. About a quarter of our students are first-
generation college students, and well over half of them have unmet financial needs. The skills and
credentials we provide to our BA and Certificate students are substantial contributors to social and
economic mobility.

Our MA program attracts and retains high-quality students who typically finish their degree in under two
years. Time to degree for our MA recipients averaged 1.88 years over the study period, and 93% of our
MA graduates report being “Satisfied” or “Very Satisfied” (on a five response scale) with their academic
experience at ECU and preparation for anthropological practice.

Public Service: In the BA, our general education courses expand the world for hundreds of ECU
students each year. Across the BA and Certificates, our faculty and students conduct research that
helps the public through facilitating sustainable coastal development, reducing regional health
disparities, historically contextualizing human disease, helping solve medicolegal death investigations,
advancing understanding of human biological and behavioral diversity through research on primates
and human populations, and fostering appreciation of regional and international cultural heritage.

MA students regularly take part in public-facing research projects that often double as the foundation
for their practicum or thesis work, such as excavations at culturally significant North Carolina sites,
examining local perspectives on environmental change and tourism, and working closely with faculty
and law enforcement on forensic investigations, aiding in body recovery and analysis.

Across programs our graduates work in a broad array of in-demand public service-related roles,
including required archaeological survey of publicly-funded construction, medicolegal death
investigation, social services agency management, teaching and educational administration, clinical
and public health, and historical interpretation. Our graduates’ skills are in demand across the region,
and opportunities for departmental growth are strong.

Regional Transformation: Growth in our region requires anthropologists. Cultural Resource
Management (CRM) archaeologists conduct required surveys before new highways, schools, and other
publicly-funded facilities are built. Cultural anthropologists with expertise in community development
manage social services agencies and help businesses attract and retain clients. Biological
anthropologists help with death investigation, train law enforcement personnel, and provide in-demand
research analyst skills in the bioengineering, medical and pharmaceutical sectors, among many others.

community agencies; student engagement in medicolegal death and missing persons investigations;
and local internships with cultural resource management agencies, museums, and Medical Examiners

ECU’s LinkedIn page shows over 450 anthropology alumni in eastern North Carolina and the

ECU anthropology alumni are particularly well-placed across the region and state in cultural resource

Strengths and Weaknesses

The department has lost five faculty members during the study period and has hired two. This net loss,
especially of archaeology faculty with expertise in cultural resource management and the archaeology
of this region, is our department’s most pressing weakness.

Anthropology BA enrollment is down 26.6% from Fall 18 to Fall 24. ECU full-time undergraduate
enrollment is down 13.2% during the same time period. The departmental decline is non-linear and is
exacerbated by the retirement of two faculty members (in 2021), both cultural anthropologists who were
particularly strong in undergraduate student advising and recruitment.

Since the 17/18 academic year, the number of graduate students has increased from 14 to 21 (in Fall
25). Increased assistantship funding rates—from $9,000 in 17/18 to $14,000 in 25/26—have improved
our competitiveness in graduate recruitment. Graduate assistantships at ECU do not include tuition
awards.

CRM Certificate enrollment has grown significantly but is negatively affected by the retirement of two
CRM archaeologists in 2024 and 2025. Forensic certificate enrollment has grown over the study period.
Global Cross-Cultural Competency Certificate enrollment is near zero.

Undergraduate course D/F/W rates averaged 14.6% from 21/22 through 23/24. These rates are lower
than the THCAS overall average rate of 22.3% during the same time period. Time to degree for our BA
recipients has averaged 3.73 academic years during the study period.

The department has averaged 832.3 student credit hours (SCH) per faculty FTE from 21/22 through
24/25. This is consistently above the College of Arts and Sciences median (740). On average, the
department has taught 6531.6 SCHs/year in 1000-level courses over the study period (67.2% of all
SCHs taught). This heavy general education service load includes significant contributions to the
University’s social science and (former) global diversity requirements, and is seen as compensation in
part for lower major and graduate student numbers.

During the study period anthropology faculty submitted a total of 45 external funding proposals as
PI/co-PI, totaling $14.4 million. Of those 19 were funded for a total of $967,245. Anthropology ranked
5th in Harriot College in total dollar amount of proposal submissions in 24/25 ($1.98M, some of which

and our campus, regional, and national reputation.

Major Findings

The self-study has provided valuable opportunity for reflection and planning as our department
embraces a new applied/career-based focus. The study underscores our perceived need to update and
optimize program offerings to attract students in an era of declining resources. Recent rertirements
leave us unable to continue strong undergraduate and MA-level offerings in archaeology related to
North America and Cultural Resources Management. The viability of the CRM Certificate is a new
concern, and we are missing opportunities to meet student demand for MA training in CRM
acchaeology, an historic strength of our department. We’ve learned, however, that student interest, plus
ECU’s investment in a new forensic anthropologist, has allowed significant growth in biological/forensic
anthropology: SCH generation in our Intro. to Biological Anthropology (ANTH/BIOL 2015) course
increased from 495 in 18/19 to 771 in 23/24 and 1533 in 24/25, and strong bio/forensic anthropology
interest has allowed our MA program to grow despite our recent inability to train CRM archaeologists.

The self-study has also allowed ample consideration of departmental needs in terms of personnel,
resources, curricular change and more significant community engagement as a high-impact learning
practice. Finally, the study highlights the strong teaching, research and service work already being
done by our faculty, providing exemplars for good work ahead.

1. Program Purpose

BA Anthropology
1.1. Program Purpose (BA)
The East Carolina University (ECU) Department of Anthropology offers a global view of human culture,
evolution, adaptation, and history to promote comparative understanding of the archaeological,
biological, and cultural aspects of humanity. To  g  e  t  h  e  r  ,  these studies nurture respect for the biological as
well as the ethnic and cultural variation present in human populations today and throughout time.

BA Anthropology students are prepared to serve society by applying methods of anthropological inquiry
across a wide and ever-emerging array of problems, questions, and career paths. Our degree program
enables students to recognize the diversity of the world’s peoples (past and present), prepares them to
be effective at communicating cross-culturally and within multicultural settings, and equips them to
apply the critical thinking skills and knowledge learned in Anthropology to a broad array of careers in
local and global settings. Students have access to high impact learning practices specific to
anthropological subdisciplines, allowing them to further develop desirable career and citizenship skills.

1.2. Program Alignment (BA)
Student Success: Anthropologists are problem solvers, and our department aspires to train students
to manage complex challenges in workplaces and communities today, but also to identify, assess and
solve problems through the decades as their careers and lives unfold. Our focus on career
development, outreach, and skills training is designed to give students the methodological tools to
succeed in a broad array of domains of application, whether those students are seeking broad
anthropological training (such as in our BA or MA) or more narrow focus aligned with another program
of study (such as our Anthropology minor, Medical Anthropology minor, or certificates in Cultural
Resources Management, Forensic Anthropology, or Global Cross-Cultural Competency). We are
actively refining our curricula to achieve alignment with our vision and have begun the process with a
faculty retreat and participation in the Anthropology Career Readiness Network’s Departmental
Advisory Initiative (ACRN DAI).

Our time to degree is low and surveyed students report high levels of postgraduate success
(employment or post-graduate education), though response rates are lower than we’d like. About a
quarter of our students are first generation college students and well over half of them have unmet
financial needs. The skills and credentials we provide to our students are substantial contributors to
social and economic mobility.

Public Service: Anthropology by its very nature promotes the values of cultural understanding in the
campus community and the region. Our general education courses expand the world for hundreds of
ECU students each year. Our faculty and students conduct research that helps the public through
facilitating sustainable coastal development, reducing regional health disparities, historically
contextualizing human disease, helping solve medicolegal death investigations, advancing
understanding of human biological and behavioral diversity through research on primates and human
populations, and fostering appreciation of regional and international cultural heritage. Our graduates
are working in a broad array of positions in cultural resource management, education, social services,
health, and technology in private and state and federal government sectors, each of which contributes
to a strong departmental legacy of applying the anthropological endeavor in service to local and global
publics.

1.3 Unique Features (BA)
Our program provides transformative experiences for students through high impact learning practices
that range from participating in forensic investigations to taking part in field experiences both locally and
abroad. We have engaged undergraduate students in research collaborations with faculty curating
archaeological collections, researching primate and human interactions, and engaging in health
services research. We have established a clear undergraduate internship pathway with the Queen
Anne’s Revenge Conservation Lab (run by the North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural
Resources, or NC DNCR) on ECU’s West Research Campus. We have ongoing study abroad
programs emphasizing field research in Medical Anthropology in Peru and Ethnoprimatology in Bali,
and until just this year we held an eastern North Carolina archaeological field school (for undergraduate
and graduate students) each summer. Anthropology has long been a major contributor to the Global
Understanding program at ECU, which enables our students to interact via videoconferencing and chat
with students from different cultures.

Our department largely focuses on three of the four major subfields in anthropology (cultural
anthropology, archaeology, and biological anthropology), although cross-listed coursework in linguistic
anthropology may be offered through the English Department based on faculty availability. Significant
planning and external collaboration efforts 24/25 helped us clarify a focus on applied anthropology as
articulated through enhanced discussion of careers and problem solving. We worked with the
Anthropology Career Readiness Network’s Departmental Advisory Initiative (ACRN DAI) to begin
planning and implementing curriculum and pedagogical transitions to this end. (Appendix A: ACRN DAI
Implementation Plan) The department benefits from anthropology’s interdisciplinary nature, which
creates bridges to other programs and academic pursuits. Two of our faculty have joint appointments:
one with Public Health and one with the Institute for Coastal Science Policy (ICSP). Faculty scholarship
additionally transforms the region through initiatives such as sustainable coastal development, reducing
health disparities, cultural heritage promotion, compliance with federal historical preservation laws, and
understanding of variation in human growth and development in eastern North Carolina. Our students

1.8 Contribution to Critical Professions (BA)
ECU’s undergraduate anthropology program lays a foundation supporting the health, educational
attainment, and quality of life of North Carolinians. The Anthropology program utilizes an integrated
approach to cultural, biological, and archaeological anthropology courses, taught by caring faculty
with a focus on career preparation and high-impact educational practices. The undergraduate
Anthropology program contributes to the social science education and pre-professional degrees of
the future health professionals, mental health practitioners, public health experts, legal experts, and
educators who serve the people of North Carolina. The program holistically prepares helping
professionals by training them to creatively solve human problems whose solutions derive from an
integrated and holistic understanding of human culture, human biology, and the human past.
Whether entering the North Carolina job market right after graduation or continuing to a
professional/graduate program, students who have majored, minored, or even just taken a class or
two in Anthropology will contribute positively to the wellbeing of their fellow North Carolinians with
the problem-solving perspective they gain in our department.

MA Anthropology
1.1 Program Purpose (MA)
The Master of Arts in Anthropology is a competitive, research and skill-intensive graduate program that
provides graduates with in-depth training in three core areas of the discipline: cultural anthropology,
biological anthropology, and archaeology. Students also gain specialized skills tailored to their unique
interests, whether in statistics, public health, forensic anthropology, primatology, bioarchaeology,
archaeology and conservation, or allied topics.

Degree recipients are equipped with the experience and ability to immediately contribute to career
domains in CRM archaeology and heritage management, public health and social services, forensic
science, federal and state government analysis, and educational administration. Flexible tracks,
including internship and practicum options, aid in career preparation and complement traditional
research-based experience.

1.2 Program Alignment (MA)

retention and timely graduation. The program exemplifies student success in terms of attracting and

cultures in Jordan, Israel, South Africa, Palau, and Madagascar.

preservation. MA graduates find roles with CRM firms, local schools, state and federal agencies, local
social services agencies, tech firms, medical research and death investigation, and in the corporate
world, or go on to pursue PhDs at other universities. ECU anthropology alumni are particularly well-
placed across the region and state in cultural resource management, conservation, historic
interpretation, and higher education administration.

1.6 Student Outcomes (MA)
Our program delivers strong student outcomes, both during the course of study and post-graduation.
We maintain an impressive second-year persistence rate of 93%, and among the 56 graduates since
17/18 the average time to degree is just under two years (1.98)—a testament to our program's
structure, support systems, and faculty commitment.

Our alumni enter the field with competitive credentials that reflect both academic excellence and
applied relevance. Employers consistently commend their readiness, noting their methodological
proficiency, research publications, and professional presentations at national and international
conferences.

Equally important is the impact of our program on student lives. Alumni frequently credit their success
to the transformative experiences they had here, highlighting the strength of our mentoring, the rigor of
our curriculum, and meaningful opportunities for scholarly engagement. These outcomes underscore
our program’s value—not only as a launching pad for professional careers, but as a model for
impactful, student-centered graduate education.

In Spring 2024 the Anthropology MA program was flagged by the state for falling below a newly
constructed Return on Investment (RoI) threshold. Specifically, the MA Anthropology Program was
flagged via calculation of Student ROI. Calculations were limited to data from the four MA graduates in
19/20 residing in NC. The timing and limitations of the study thus excluded the successes of students
graduating before or after that year, or who found gainful and rewarding employment across the country
or the globe.  The designation afforded us the opportunity to create an improvement plan for time to
degree while showcasing our departmental commitment to strong student mentorship. We have revised
admissions review procedures and advising practices, enhanced alumni interaction/networking, and
enhanced graduate student support. Enhanced support includes an increase in assistantship amounts
from $10,000 to $14,000/academic year, conference registration funding for all presenting MA students,
and significant external fundraising to support the same. Additionally, in Fall 24 we instituted a “Midterm
Mentoring” program wherein all MA students meet with their advisor and the Graduate Director or Chair
each term to discuss current progress and any challenges, strategize thesis or non-thesis pathways
aligned with developing career aspirations, and receive advice for post-graduate preparation. These
improvements are all designed to ensure timely degree completion, but also to provide students with
clear mentorship, networking opportunities, and skills necessary to succeed on the job market.

Certificate in Cultural Resources Management (CRM)
1.1. Certificate Purpose (CRM)
The premise of the CRM certificate is that changes in federal and state laws as well as public interest
over the last few decades have been significant enough to warrant development of an explicit program
aligning with archaeology becoming a professional applied career option.  Broadly speaking, when
completed, the certificate provides students with a basic level of competency to pursue an entry-level
job in either the public or private sector of archaeology or be equally prepared to continue their
education in graduate school. It includes skills preparation options in GIS and public history and
museum studies.

1.2 Certificate alignment (CRM)
When originally proposed, the certificate was created to correspond with at least one goal in ECU’s
strategic plan: “education for a new century.” To  d  a  y  ,  t  h  e  c  e  r  t  i  f  i  c  a  t  e  i  s  a  l  s  o  c  o  n  s  i  s  t  e  n  t  w  i  t  h  t  h  e  E  C  U  ’  s
goals of “maximizing student success” and “public service.” This certificate maximizes student success
by providing job training while also serving the public in that most of these jobs are related to historic
preservation—the latter being of keen interest to the public in the 21st century. In addition, CRM is
required by historic preservation laws and involves archaeologists employed by either federal or state
agencies or by private firms who assist in compliance with these laws.

1.3 Unique features (CRM)
This certificate is distinctive in that it is tailored to students in our archaeology program. As such, it can
be considered an “applied track.” It thus makes us more competitive with other universities by providing
students with a specific curriculum designed to provide them with the skills to pursue archaeology jobs
or a graduate degree.

The CRM certificate has had between 2 (Fall 18) and 10 (Fall 21) students enrolled during the study

Certificate in Forensic Anthropology
1.1  Certificate Purpose (Forensic)
The purpose of the Forensic Anthropology Certificate is to equip students with introductory skills and
knowledge leading toward competency in forensic anthropological application. These skills include
human anatomy, basic forensic science and evidence handling, expert witness testimony, professional
standardization and ethics, field recovery, determination of medicolegal significance, forensic
taphonomy, biological profile techniques leading towards personal identification, and the use of
statistics in human identification applications. Upon completion, the certificate provides students with a
basic level of competency applicable to entry-level jobs in either the public- or private sector in the field
of death investigation and/or broader forensic investigative practices. Further, completion of the
certificate prepares students for graduate training across anthropology or the forensic sciences and
provides the introductory skills necessary for professional training in medicine, dentistry, or nursing.

1.2 Certificate Alignment (Forensic)
The Forensic Anthropology Certificate directly contributes to the institution's mission by equipping
students with specialized skills that not only serve the local and global economy but also foster public
service and regional transformation. Through hands-on training and research, students help solve real-
world issues related to justice, public safety, and human rights, thereby improving quality of life locally
and globally. Further, and in line with regional transformation and the associated priority of outcomes in
rural communities, skills learned are translatable to a criminal justice / forensic science career paths in
local eastern NC medicolegal settings where specialized training may be lacking.

1.3 Unique Features (Forensic)
ECU was a pioneer in offering forensic anthropology certification to undergraduate students. Several
other universities now have similar programs, but our certificate continues to help us more clearly
attract students with interest in forensic anthropology, plus it allows students (particularly those with
interest in criminal justice or biology) to specialize in an anthropological sub-discipline. It also

In our increasingly globalized and interconnected world, being able to understand and negotiate cultural
differences is a critical skill that will allow for success in a broad array of career paths. For students to
be successful, serve the public, and help promote regional transformation, they will need to understand
differences across cultural groups and apply that knowledge in their professional and personal lives.

1.3 Unique Features (Global CCC)
This is the only certificate program at East Carolina University that is open to students in all fields who
wish to build cross-cultural competence. It combines courses that build awareness of cultural
differences with expertise in research methods to collect data on cultural difference as well as to
contribute to workplaces that can benefit from multicultural understanding in problem-solving, service
provision, and product development.

1.4 Student Demand (Global CCC)
The Global Cross-Cultural Competency certificate has had between 1 (Fall 23) and 21 (Spring 20)
students enrolled during the study period, and 0 as of Spring 25 (two students have enrolled for Fall
25). The Spring 21 retirement of two cultural anthropologists in the department greatly reduced the
number of elective courses we have been able to offer in this certificate area, and much of the demand
for the certificate was tied to their advising.

1.5 Workforce Demand (Global CCC)
The Global Cross-Cultural Competency Certificate is not tied to any specific employment area, so
workforce demand measurement is difficult to construct. That said, reframing (and likely renaming) of
the certificate could allow it to more directly serve students with interests in business, education, and
the health professions.

1.6 Student Outcomes (Global CCC)
ECU Post-Graduation survey participation among Global Cross-Cultural Competency Certificate
graduates is too scant to allow for meaningful interpretation of outcomes, but anecdotally we can
confirm a positive track record of employment or graduate program placement for these graduates.

1.7 Program Costs and Productivity (Global CCC)
Please see BA section 1.7, above, as cost and productivity data are analyzed at the department level.

1.8 Contribution to Critical Professions (Global CCC)
The ability to understand and cooperate with individuals from diverse backgrounds is a critical skill for
those working in sectors that are important for the well-being and quality of life of all North Carolinians,
such as health care and education. For example, multicultural understanding allows public health and
medical professionals to effectively communicate with all patients, contributing to improved health
outcomes. Similarly, understanding how culture influences learning, behavior, and child development
helps educators and staff design culturally relevant and effective teaching materials and assessments.

We plan significant undergraduate and graduate curriculum and course content changes aligned with
improved career focus as part of our ACRN DAI Implementation Plan and our goal to increase majors by

professor. In the MA Program, our new Midterm Mentoring meetings help improve student direction

a short two years to degree.

BA-Anthropology
3.1 Degree Requirements (BA)
The BA in Anthropology prepares students with skills and perspectives needed to succeed in a
globalized world by fostering cross-cultural understanding and critical thinking. Students begin with
2000-level courses in cultural anthropology, archaeology, and biological anthropology (with a lab), then
advance to 3000- and 4000-level courses, including at least one required methods course and electives
on specialized topics. Students also complete a minor, foreign language study, and general education.
The program maintains high retention and graduation rates, strong student satisfaction, and consistent
four-year degree completion.

3.2 Approaches to Curriculum and Innovative Practices (BA)
The department keeps its curriculum current through regular faculty reviews, integration of new
research, and responsiveness to student feedback. Faculty assess course offerings, learning
outcomes, and program goals to ensure alignment with disciplinary developments and best practices.

The program emphasizes hands-on learning through field schools, laboratory experience, and
community project participation. Students gain experience in local initiatives such as the Ayden African
American Cemetery Project and the Bath historical archaeology field school, as well as international
programs in Medical Anthropology (Peru) and Ethnoprimatology (Bali). Laboratory training in
archaeology, biological anthropology, and forensics provides additional practical skills through work on
artifact curation, skeletal analysis, and primate research.

Global engagement is fostered through ECU’s Global Understanding program, which connects students
with peers worldwide for cross-cultural dialogue. The department also employs equitable teaching and
assessment practices, using inclusive materials, transparent assignments, and varied assessments
such as collaborative projects, reflective writing, and community-based research. These experiences
help students apply theory in real-world contexts and build professional competencies.

understanding of core concepts and methods. To strengthen kinship and the culture concept, additional

In Biological Anthropology, only 48% met the benchmark in 23/24. While improvements were noted

Certificate in Cultural Resources Management
3.1 Degree Map and Course Sequences (CRM)
The Certificate in Cultural Resources Management (CRM) is designed to progressively build student
knowledge and skills through a structured sequence of prerequisites and advanced coursework.
Students must maintain a minimum 2.5 GPA for admission and throughout the program, which requires
at least 18 semester credit hours.

3.2 Approaches to Curriculum and Innovative Practices (CRM)
The CRM certificate curriculum has heretofore been kept current through faculty expertise, ongoing
engagement with the discipline, and integration of emerging technologies and legislation. Faculty
teaching the core courses — ANTH 3077 (Archaeological Methods) and ANTH 3175 (Archaeological
Field Training) — draw on extensive fieldwork and research experience to introduce students to
contemporary methods, tools, and legal frameworks.

Innovative approaches include using tools such as Google Earth to identify archaeological sites in arid
environments, incorporating the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990) and its
2023 revisions, and training students on field technologies like the total station.

3.13 Additional Resources (CRM)
To implement the planned improvements to the CRM Certificate and enhance student learning and
satisfaction, the Department of Anthropology requires additional faculty and support resources.

Two faculty members specializing in North American prehistory and historical archaeology have retired,
leaving six key courses untaught: the core course (ANTH 3175 — Field Methods in Archaeology) and
electives (ANTH 3115, 3116, 5120, 5126, and 3900). No current faculty are qualified to teach these
courses or to lead a local archaeological field school. This faculty gap has had a cascade effect: without
a trained North American archaeologist to oversee the field school, ECU students no longer have
access to an affordable local fieldwork opportunity.

The loss of the field school has priced many students out of experiential learning. Although ECU’s field
school was significantly more affordable ($2,500–$3,000) than comparable U.S. and international
programs ($5,500–$8,000), students must now enroll in external programs at much higher costs.

To address these challenges, the department needs:

• At least one full-time faculty hire with expertise in North American archaeology and CRM to restore
the teaching of core and elective courses, to lead the local field school, and to ensure ongoing
NAGPRA compliance and archival best pratices.

• Continued and ultimately expanded funding for field and laboratory facilities, equipment, and supplies
to support hands-on learning. The current archaeology lab budget is $2446/year. Ed Tech fees can
potentially be used to support teaching-related equipment needs. The department charges no lab fees
(opportunities to introduce new fees at ECU are highly constrained).

• Modest support for scholarships and student aid to offset the costs of fieldwork participation. Existing
anthropology scholarships total less than $100k in available spendable balances and some have
restrictions on how they are used, so raising $250,000 dollars to support students with another $10,000
per year for fieldwork experiences would be a worthwhile goal, particularly in light of increasing vehicle
and supply expenses.

These resources would be highly beneficial in re-establishing the CRM Certificate’s integrity, providing
students with accessible, high-quality training, and ensuring they are competitive in the cultural
resource management job market. In turn, we would be able to significantly increase the draw of
archaeology-interested students to the department using our uniquely strong relationships with major
archaeological employers in the region.

### Courses

**[ANTH 101 Introduction to Anthropology credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/101)**

Anthropology was first envisioned as a holistic discipline, combining insights from the study of human anatomy and evolution, research on material remains of human settlements, and the analysis of social interaction in language and other cultural practices. Following this tradition, this course explores the questions about where humans came from, how societies live and communicate, and why human cultural groups vary.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Social & Beh Sci - Soc Sci  
Cultural Studies - Western

**[ANTH 102 Human Origins and Culture credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/102)**

Explores the origin and evolution of humans with an emphasis on reconstructing and interpreting fossil evidence. It provides an introduction to the fundamentals of biological anthropology and draws on a diverse range of other disciplines that contribute to the study of human evolution – evolutionary biology, population genetics, comparative anatomy, primatology, archaeology, geology and paleoecology. We examine the fossil and artifact record of the last several million years in order to develop an understanding of why we are interesting animals and a somewhat unique species.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Social & Beh Sci - Soc Sci

**[ANTH 103 Anthro in a Changing World credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/103)**

[IAI Code: S1901N] Presents the fundamental areas of anthropological analysis through a series of comparative cases that emphasize social and cultural relations in global contexts. Directs attention to the anthropological history of global empires and colonial states, their cultural exchanges, and contemporary studies of culture, society, and globalization.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Cultural Studies - Non-West  
Social & Beh Sci - Soc Sci

**[ANTH 104 Talking Culture credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/104)**

Introduces you to language-in-use from the perspective of linguistic anthropology. We explore how the language(s) people use creates a specific "worldview" or cultural "common sense" and how this creates and maintains distinct concepts of self, society and culture. We will examine critically the ways in which differences in language and communication work in the USA in relation to power and politics, the media, gender, ethnicity/race, age, class, and identity, with comparisons to other cultures. During the semester you will encounter new information about language structure and use, and learn methods of investigation and analysis used in contemporary linguistic anthropology. Same as [LING 104](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=LING%20104 "LING 104").   
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Social & Beh Sci - Soc Sci

**[ANTH 105 World Archaeology credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/105)**

Using archaeological data, traces our prehistoric heritage and the processes which led to the evolution of agriculture, settled villages, and civilization in many areas of the world. Lectures range from the earliest Homo sapiens to Sumeria, Egypt, Mexico, Peru, and the United States.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Humanities - Hist & Phil

**[ANTH 106 Hist Arch Americas credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/106)**

Explores recent theoretical, methodological, and thematic developments in historical archaeology in North America and the Caribbean. The temporal coverage is 1500-1900 AD. Examines how historical archaeologists use artifactual, documentary and oral history evidence in interpreting the past, and how historical archaeology can contribute to our understanding of the ways by which material culture can be used to study race, class, gender, and ethnic identities. Same as [AFRO 106](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=AFRO%20106 "AFRO 106").  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Humanities - Hist & Phil  
Cultural Studies - US Minority

**[ANTH 108 Religion & Society in West I credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/108)**

See [REL 108](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=REL%20108 "REL 108").  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Humanities - Hist & Phil  
Cultural Studies - Western

**[ANTH 109 Religion & Society in West II credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/109)**

Same as [PHIL 109](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=PHIL%20109 "PHIL 109") and [REL 109](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=REL%20109 "REL 109"). See [REL 109](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=REL%20109 "REL 109").  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Humanities - Hist & Phil  
Cultural Studies - Western

**[ANTH 110 Humanizing Science credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/110)**

Scientists are often taught that the skills they need are confined to conducting research in the lab, the field, or the observatory. Yet science is also a human endeavor. If scientists are not taught this lesson, mistakes can be made that have real implications for people's lives, for scientific progress, and for who gets to be a scientist. Therefore this course will introduce 1) a brief history of Western and non-Western science, 2) the influences of social categories and oppressions on scientific advancement, 3) the incentive and reward structure of science, and 4) stories of scientists who have chosen to walk a brave path in the way they conduct and disseminate their research. We will engage in a mix of ethnographic and case study work and bring interpretive and systematic analysis to bear on what it means to be a scientist. The ultimate goal of the course is to provide a substantive, rigorous, and broad introduction to the culture of science, and how that culture affects the people of science, its practice, and its process.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Social & Beh Sci - Soc Sci

**[ANTH 112 Language, Race, and Ethnicity in the United States credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/112)**

Exploring historical, cultural, and theoretical perspectives on the relationship between language, race, and ethnicity in the United States, we ask, what is 'race' and 'ethnicity', and how do ideas about racial and ethnic belonging and difference relate to ideas about language? We examine how language use reflects, reproduces, and/or challenges racial and ethnic boundaries and explore topics such as language and racial/ethnic identity-making, language and nationalism, bilingual/multilingual education, and language and racial humor.

**[ANTH 126 Humans and Animals - Food or Friend? credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/126)**

Emphasizes questions of how we can move toward a more sustainable future by focusing on two key realms of human relations with non-human animals: as food, and as “friend,” or pets/companion animals. Anchored in humanistic social science, this course also exposes students to the benefits and challenges of interdisciplinary thinking and research, and provides an opportunity for active experiential learning and public engagement Prerequisite: This course is intended for first and second year students.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Social & Beh Sci - Soc Sci

**[ANTH 130 History of South Asia credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/130)**

Same as [HIST 130](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=HIST%20130 "HIST 130"). See [HIST 130](https://catalog.illinois.edu/search/?P=HIST%20130 "HIST 130").  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Humanities - Hist & Phil  
Cultural Studies - Non-West

**[ANTH 143 Biology of Human Behavior credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/143)**

Biological anthropology looks at human biology and behavior through the lens of evolutionary biology. However, as human behavior is complex, it cannot be understood independent of culture or the physical environment. We will explore how biology intersects with environmental factors, including culture, to influence human behavior. Students will learn the skills needed to become scientifically literate, learning their place in nature, the importance of the comparative method in learning about ourselves, and the interaction between biology and culture in understanding the human condition. Topics include evolutionary theory and human evolution, primate origins of human behaviors, social and sexual behaviors, aggression, cooperation, and language, cognition, and culture. This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Nat Sci & Tech - Life Sciences

**[ANTH 157 The Archaeology of Illinois credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/157)**

Traces the prehistory of Illinois from the first entry of people into the region more than 13,000 years ago until the 17th century and the beginning of historical records; examines subsequent cultural changes up to the 19th century and statehood from an archaeological and ethnohistorical perspective.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Humanities - Hist & Phil

**[ANTH 160 Race and Contemporary Social Issues credit: 3 Hours.](https://courses.illinois.edu/schedule/terms/ANTH/160)**

Engages with issues such as migration, borders, policing and related topics to examine certain key interventions in the analysis of race in the United States. Introduces students to critical methods and theories in socio-cultural anthropology and allied disciplines in order to grapple with these issues. We will read a variety of material, including ethnographic accounts, scholarly and popular articles, and a work that blurs non-fiction with fiction-writing, as well as screening related films and documentaries. Students will develop a conceptual vocabulary (keywords) to begin analyzing the social problem that race and racism has become in US society.  
This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for:  
Cultural Studies - US Minority
